notes.h: Climate as a resource and a constraint
notes.b: Climate is both a resource and a limit. Temperature, the amount of rainfall, its seasonal timing and its reliability, sunshine and wind decide what can be grown, how much water is available, where tourists go and what it costs to adapt.
points: Rich economies can overcome climatic limits with technology: irrigation (supplying water to crops by channels or pipes), reservoirs, desalination (removing salt from seawater) and snow-making. They can afford to pay for these.
Poor economies that depend on rain-fed farming (crops watered only by rainfall) are the most exposed, because they have no stored or piped water to fall back on when the rain fails.
Climate change is shifting all of these. Its evidence and causes are taught in the notes on climatic environments and climate change.
notes.tip: Examiners want a judgement, so say that climate influences development but wealth and technology modify the influence. Avoid saying climate determines development.

notes.h: Irish agriculture: grassland and regional contrasts
notes.b: Ireland's rainfall and mild temperatures give a long grass-growing season, so grass is the most important crop. Most farmland is grassland, used for dairy, beef and sheep (pastoral farming, meaning rearing animals). Rainfall and soils then split the country into farming regions.
points: Grass grows when soil temperature is above about 6 °C. In Ireland's mild climate that is for most of the year, and the season is longest in the south and south-west.

Annual rainfall is about 750 mm in the driest east, about 1,000–1,250 mm across much of the west and over 2,000 mm on many western mountains. This is why farming differs so much between east and west.
The south and east are drier and sunnier, and the south-east is the sunniest region. The 2020 Census of Agriculture counted about 135,000 farms.

Tillage (growing crops on ploughed land) is concentrated in the drier south and east, e.g. Co. Wexford, Co. Carlow and Co. Kildare. Barley, wheat, oats, potatoes and vegetables can be harvested there in dry conditions.

The Golden Vale (Co. Tipperary and Co. Limerick) has moderate rainfall and good soils on brown earths (well-drained fertile soils), which suit intensive dairying. EU milk quotas (limits on milk output) ended in 2015, after which dairying expanded.

Gley soils (waterlogged, poorly drained soils) of the drumlin belt (the lowland of low hills in Co. Cavan, Co. Monaghan and Co. Leitrim) and Co. Clare carry mainly grass for cattle, with a short grazing season.

The very wet west and north-west, with poorly drained gley and peat soils, suit mainly beef and sheep rearing on rough grazing, with small farms and low incomes. There is more on this in the notes on a peripheral Irish region.
notes.tip: For the regional contrast, give one region per type of farming with its reason: tillage in the dry south and east, dairying in the Golden Vale, beef and sheep in the wet west.

notes.h: Irish agriculture: problems of too much rain
notes.b: Too much rain is as much a problem for Irish farming as too little. Wet weather raises costs, delays work and spreads disease.
points: Waterlogged soils are poached (trampled into mud) by cattle, and the grazing season is shortened. Animals must then be housed and fed silage (stored fermented grass) for longer, which raises costs.
Wet spells make it hard to make silage and hay and to harvest cereals, because the crops cannot be cut and dried in dry conditions.

Heavy rain leaches nutrients from the soil (washes them down out of reach of roots), and slurry (liquid animal manure) runs off when it rains after spreading. There is more on this in the notes on environmental pollution.
Damp weather favours diseases: potato blight, and liver fluke (a parasite) in sheep and cattle.
The summer of 2012 was exceptionally wet in Ireland. Poor silage and hay harvests, followed by a cold, late spring in 2013, caused a fodder (animal feed) crisis in spring 2013.
Farmers ran out of feed in spring 2013. Fodder was imported, including from Britain and France, and the Government funded a fodder transport subsidy.
The Great Famine (1845–49) followed potato blight, a disease favoured by mild, damp weather.
notes.tip: Give both sides, too much rain and too little, when asked about rainfall and Irish farming. Do not quote rainfall or temperature figures for 2012 or 2013.

notes.h: Irish agriculture: problems of too little rain
notes.b: Ireland is a wet country, but dry spells also hurt farmers because grass is the crop that feeds the animals.
points: Grass stops growing in prolonged dry spells, so farmers have to feed winter fodder (stored feed) in summer.
Milk yields fall, and fodder runs short the following winter because the winter feed was used up in summer. Light soils (free-draining soils that dry out fast) of the south-east suffer most.

Summer 2018: a long anticyclonic spell (settled high-pressure weather) from late May to mid-July brought heat and drought to Ireland. Met Éireann, the national weather service, recorded absolute drought (a spell with almost no rain) at many stations.
Grass growth almost stopped that summer. Teagasc (the agriculture and food development authority) and the Government organised fodder imports and supports for the following winter.
notes.tip: Use the 2018 drought as the example of too little rain, and do not quote rainfall or temperature figures for it.

notes.b: Climate change brings both gains and risks to Irish farming, and farming is itself a source of the gases that cause it.
points: Warmer temperatures lengthen the growing season, and maize and other crops become more feasible. Wetter winters and more frequent summer droughts add risk.

Agriculture produces over a third of Ireland's greenhouse gas emissions (EPA, early 2020s). The EPA is the Environmental Protection Agency. There is more on this in the notes on environmental pollution.

notes.b: In India, farming follows the monsoon, the seasonal wind that brings the summer rains. When the rains arrive, and how strong they are, set the farming year.
points: The south-west monsoon reaches Kerala around 1 June, covers India by mid-July and brings about three-quarters of the annual rainfall.

Kharif (summer) crops such as rice and cotton are sown with the monsoon rains. Rabi (winter) crops such as wheat rely on stored water, irrigation and western disturbances (winter rain-bearing weather systems).
A late or weak monsoon cuts harvests, farm incomes and GDP (the value of what the country produces), because so much of the year's water arrives in one season.

The Green Revolution (high-yielding crop varieties) from the mid-1960s, in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh, relied on irrigation. Canal irrigation in Punjab and Haryana brought salinisation (salt building up in the soil) and waterlogging.
The Indira Gandhi Canal in Rajasthan carries irrigation water into the dry north-west.

notes.h: Global example: Egypt and the Nile
notes.b: Egypt shows a country with almost no rain of its own, so farming depends entirely on one river. A dam turned an unpredictable flood into a controlled supply, but at a cost.
points: Egypt is almost rainless, so farming depends on irrigation from the Nile. The green strip of the Nile valley and delta shows through the desert.
The Nile's flood came from summer rain far upstream, and its uncertainty ended when the Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970.
The dam created Lake Nasser, one of the world's largest reservoirs. This allows year-round (perennial) irrigation, more than one crop a year and hydroelectricity (electricity from flowing water).
Costs: the fertile silt is trapped behind the dam, so farmers need artificial fertiliser. Salinisation and waterlogging have spread, and the delta is eroding.
notes.tip: The Aswan High Dam (1970) is not the same as the older Aswan Low Dam, so name the High Dam.

notes.b: California's Central Valley is a farming region where the summers are dry, so its high-value crops depend on irrigation. It shows what happens when drought cuts that supply.
points: California's Central Valley is one of the world's most productive farming regions. Its dry summers mean that high-value fruit, nuts and vegetables depend on irrigation.
Irrigation comes from large state and federal water projects, which carry snowmelt from the mountains, and from groundwater (water pumped from underground).
In the drought of about 2012–2016, farmers left land fallow (unplanted) and over-pumped groundwater. Heavy groundwater pumping caused land subsidence (the ground sinking) in the valley.
Governor Jerry Brown ordered a mandatory 25% cut in urban water use in April 2015, so cities as well as farms had to cut their water use.
notes.tip: Do not give output figures for California's farming.

notes.h: Global example: rain-fed farming in the Sahel and rainfall reliability
notes.b: In the Sahel, the dry belt south of the Sahara, crops rely on rain alone. This shows that how reliable rainfall is matters as much as how much falls.
points: The Sahel has one short wet season, in which millet and sorghum are grown alongside pastoral herding (keeping livestock).
Any shortfall in rain means crop failure, with losses of food and livestock, because farmers have no irrigation to fall back on.
Rainfall reliability matters as much as the total: the lower the average rainfall, the more variable it is from year to year. Dry regions therefore face both low and unpredictable harvests.

notes.b: Water for homes comes from rain that has collected in rivers, lakes, reservoirs and underground. So rainfall shapes how secure a household supply is, even in a wet country.
points: Domestic water depends on rainfall refilling rivers, lakes, reservoirs and groundwater. Supply must be stored to cover dry periods.
Demand peaks in hot, dry weather, exactly when supply is lowest.
Group water schemes (community-run supplies) and private wells serve many rural homes. Wells can run dry in drought and be contaminated after heavy rain.
In arid and monsoon countries, water supply depends on seasonal rain, groundwater and long-distance transfers (carrying water from one region to another).
Rich, dry countries such as the Gulf states and Israel rely heavily on desalination for domestic water.
Women and children in poor rural areas spend hours a day collecting water, which keeps girls out of school.

notes.h: Ireland's water paradox and Dublin's supply
notes.b: Ireland has plenty of rain, yet water supply is still a problem. The cause is where the rain falls compared with where people live.
points: Ireland's paradox: there is plenty of rain overall, but most of it falls in the west while most people live in the east, where rainfall is lowest (about 750 mm a year around Dublin).
Census 2022 counted about 1.45 million people in Dublin county, out of about 5.1 million in Ireland.
Old, leaking pipes waste a large share of treated water, and treatment capacity (how much water can be cleaned for drinking) is tight.
Dublin's water comes mainly from the River Liffey, through the Poulaphouca reservoir (also called the Blessington lakes, Co. Wicklow), and from the Vartry reservoir at Roundwood, Co. Wicklow.
The Water Supply Project would take water from the River Shannon at Parteen Basin, just south of Lough Derg, by a pipeline of about 170 km to the Greater Dublin Area. It is planned, not built.
Uisce Éireann (Irish Water), which adopted its name in 2023, is responsible for public water supply.
notes.tip: Ireland's water problem is not lack of rain overall. Explain it as location of demand against supply, plus storage, treatment capacity and leakage.

notes.b: The 2018 drought showed that a wet country can still run short of water for homes.
points: Irish Water imposed a hosepipe ban (a Water Conservation Order, a legal limit on using water outdoors), first in the Greater Dublin Area in early July 2018 and later extended to the whole country.
The ban shows a rainfall shortfall affecting domestic supply in a wet country.
notes.tip: Do not quote rainfall or temperature figures for 2018.

notes.h: Global example: Cape Town's Day Zero
notes.b: Cape Town came close to running out of water. It shows how a rainfall failure becomes a supply crisis, and how a city can respond.
points: Cape Town, South Africa, has a Mediterranean climate (wet winters and dry summers). Three dry winters, about 2015–2017, left its reservoirs very low.
In early 2018 the city warned of 'Day Zero', when household taps would be shut off.
From 1 February 2018 residents were limited to 50 litres per person per day, with higher tariffs (prices), reduced water pressure and public campaigns.
Day Zero was avoided after usage was roughly halved and the winter rains of 2018 returned.
Lessons: diversify supply (groundwater, recycling and desalination), reduce leaks, and plan for longer droughts.

notes.b: Drought is a long period with much less precipitation (rain, snow and other falling moisture) than normal for that place, so that water supply falls short of demand. It can be measured at three stages, from sky to soil to rivers.
points: Meteorological drought is a shortfall of rain, so it is measured by rainfall totals.
Agricultural drought is soil moisture too low for crops, so plants wilt even if some rain has fallen.
Hydrological drought is low rivers, reservoirs and groundwater, which means the water supply itself runs short.

Causes: blocking anticyclones (high-pressure systems that stay put and divert rain-bearing weather); failure or shift of the ITCZ (the belt of rising air and heavy rain near the equator) or monsoon; El Niño (a warming of the Pacific that disturbs rainfall worldwide); and climate change.
notes.tip: Define drought relative to normal for that place, and name the three types.

notes.b: Drought hits the economy through farming first, then spreads to prices, jobs, energy and public spending.
points: Crop failure and loss of livestock, because grass and crops die without water.
Higher food prices, because less is produced, and loss of farm income and rural jobs.
Famine in poor countries, and migration to cities and abroad, because people leave when farming can no longer feed them.
Less hydroelectricity and less cooling water for power stations, and river transport disrupted because water levels fall.
Wildfires, because dry vegetation burns easily, and government spending on relief.

notes.h: Drought in a developed economy: Australia
notes.b: A rich economy can absorb drought, but not without losses. The Millennium Drought in Australia shows this.
points: The Millennium Drought in south-eastern Australia lasted roughly from the late 1990s to 2009, hitting farming in the Murray–Darling Basin, Australia's main irrigated farming region.
Losses were absorbed through insurance, government aid, water trading and technology, but farm output fell and towns faced water restrictions.
Australian cities, including Melbourne, built large desalination plants in response.

Rich and poor responses contrast: a developed economy absorbs drought through insurance, aid, water trading, technology and desalination, while a poor economy with few of these faces famine. The Horn of Africa case below shows this.
notes.tip: Contrast rich and poor responses to drought. California's drought, covered earlier, also counts as a developed-economy case.

notes.h: Drought in a developing economy: the Horn of Africa, 2011
notes.b: Where people have little saving, insurance or state support, drought turns into famine. The Horn of Africa in 2011 is the example.
points: Drought across the Horn of Africa in 2011 followed two failed rainy seasons, linked to La Niña (the cool counterpart of El Niño in the Pacific).
Crops failed, livestock died and food prices soared, because the failed rains cut food supply.
The UN declared famine in parts of southern Somalia in July 2011, where conflict (al-Shabaab) blocked aid.
A later UN-backed study estimated about 260,000 deaths in Somalia, about half of them children under five.
Large numbers fled to the Dadaab camps in Kenya and to camps in Ethiopia.
Ethiopia's famine of 1983–85 followed drought and was worsened by civil war. It led to Band Aid (1984) and the Live Aid concerts (July 1985) organised by Bob Geldof.
notes.tip: Do not give death tolls for the Ethiopian or Sahel famines. The only famine figure to use is the Somalia 2011 estimate.

notes.b: Responses either warn of drought early, store or save water, or help people once it hits.
points: Early warning systems using rainfall, satellite and market data, so that governments and aid agencies can act before famine sets in.
Water storage in dams, tanks and rainwater harvesting (collecting rain from roofs and surfaces).
Drought-tolerant crops and seed varieties, which can still yield with less water.
Irrigation efficiency, such as drip irrigation (water delivered slowly to plant roots, so less is wasted).
Food aid and cash transfers, so that people can buy food; insurance, which pays out when crops fail.
Restrictions such as hosepipe bans, which cut demand; desalination, which adds a supply that does not depend on rain.

notes.b: Desertification is often misunderstood as the Sahara advancing. It is really damage to land, and climate and people together cause it.
points: Desertification is land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas caused by climatic variations and human activities (UNCCD definition, adopted 1994). The UNCCD is the UN Convention to Combat Desertification.
It is the spread of desert-like conditions, not the advance of sand dunes from the Sahara.
Drought is a climatic event; desertification is a process of land degradation that drought can trigger.
17 June is World Day to Combat Desertification.
notes.tip: Define desertification as land degradation caused by climate and people together, and not as the Sahara advancing.

notes.h: The Sahel: desertification and the economy
notes.b: The Sahel is a key example of desertification. Here the focus is on rainfall, drought and the economy: harvests, incomes, food, migration and conflict.
points: The Sahel runs from Senegal and Mauritania through Mali, Burkina Faso, Niger and Chad to Sudan. Rainfall is roughly 200–600 mm, falling in one short summer wet season when the ITCZ (the rain belt) moves north.
Droughts in the 1970s and 1980s caused failed harvests and livestock deaths.
Pastoralists (herding peoples) lost their livelihoods, and the region became dependent on food imports.
Migration to cities, including coastal cities, and abroad; conflict between herders and farmers over shrinking land and water.
Lake Chad has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s (about 90%, widely quoted), hitting fishing and farming around it.
There is more on the soil causes of Sahel degradation in the notes on human interference with soils.
notes.tip: Do not give famine death tolls for the Sahel.

notes.b: Responses to desertification range from international agreements to local farming methods that restore the land.
points: The UNCCD, adopted in 1994, coordinates international action.
The Great Green Wall, launched by the African Union in 2007, aims to run about 8,000 km from Senegal to Djibouti. Progress has been slow and well short of target.
Zaï pits (planting holes that catch rain) and stone lines (lines of stones that slow runoff) in the Yatenga region of Burkina Faso, associated with the farmer Yacouba Sawadogo.
In Niger, farmer-managed natural regeneration (farmers letting trees regrow on their land) has regreened about 5 million hectares since the 1980s.

notes.h: The Dust Bowl: desertification in a rich economy
notes.b: Desertification is not only a poor-country problem. The Dust Bowl in the United States shows drought and ploughing together wrecking farmland in a rich economy.
points: Drought on ploughed grassland in the 1930s, on the Great Plains of Oklahoma and Kansas, produced dust storms.
Farm failures and migration followed, because the dust storms stripped the land of its topsoil.

The US Soil Conservation Service, set up in 1935, promoted shelter belts (rows of trees that block wind), contour ploughing (ploughing along the slope's contours to slow runoff) and crop rotation (changing the crop each year).
The Dust Bowl shows desertification-type damage in a rich economy. There is more on its soil side in the notes on human interaction and mass movement.

notes.b: Tourists choose places for their weather, so climate is a resource that tourism can sell.
points: Sunshine, warmth, low rainfall and a warm sea attract 'sun, sea and sand' tourism.
Reliable snow attracts winter sports, and a mild climate allows outdoor activities.
Climate decides the tourist season, because visitors come when the weather suits the activity.
notes.tip: Tourism in general belongs to the economic chapters. Here, write only about how climate influences it.

notes.b: The Mediterranean is the main case of climate creating a tourist economy. The same dry summers that attract visitors also create problems.
points: Hot, dry, sunny summers have made the Mediterranean one of the world's most visited regions. Mass package tourism grew from the 1960s with cheap jet flights.
Spain received about 85 million international tourists in 2023, a record, making it the world's second most visited country after France.
Spain is the most popular foreign holiday destination for Irish people.
Benefits: jobs, foreign earnings, infrastructure and regional development. There is more on this in the notes on a peripheral European region, the Mezzogiorno.
Climate problem: tourists arrive in the driest season, so water demand from hotels, pools and golf courses peaks when supply is lowest.
Other problems: jobs are seasonal, and coasts are overdeveloped.
Protests against mass tourism took place in 2024 in the Canary Islands and in Barcelona.
notes.tip: Do not give tourism revenue figures.

notes.b: Some destinations sell warmth in winter, when northern Europe is cold. The Canary Islands do this.
points: The Canary Islands lie off north-west Africa at about 28° N.
Mild, dry winters and the cooling Canary Current (a cool ocean current) give them a year-round tourist season that attracts northern Europeans.

notes.b: Ski resorts depend on snow, so they are very sensitive to a warming climate.
points: Ski tourism depends on reliable snow cover, and it supports mountain economies in several European countries.
Climate change is raising the snow line (the height above which snow lies) and shortening seasons, so lower-altitude resorts struggle or close.
Resorts invest in artificial snow-making, which needs water, energy and cold enough nights.
Resorts also diversify into summer walking and cycling, so they earn money when there is no snow.
notes.tip: Do not give ski-season length or snow-line figures.

notes.b: Tropical islands sell warm weather and coral reefs, but the same climate brings hurricanes, bleaching and rising seas.
points: Tropical island destinations depend on warm weather and coral reefs. Their peak season is the dry season of the northern winter, and the Atlantic hurricane season (1 June to 30 November) is the low season.
Hurricane Irma, a Category 5 hurricane (the top category) in September 2017, damaged or destroyed almost every building on Barbuda. Its whole population was evacuated to Antigua.
Hurricane Maria, in September 2017, devastated Puerto Rico. An official study estimated about 3,000 deaths.
Mass bleaching of the Great Barrier Reef (corals losing their colour as stressed by warm water) has occurred repeatedly since the late 1990s, damaging reef tourism.
Sea-level rise threatens low-lying island nations such as the Maldives. There is more on this in the notes on environmental pollution.
notes.tip: Irma's damage to Barbuda and Maria's toll in Puerto Rico are separate events, so do not mix them.

notes.b: Ireland's climate is poor for beach holidays, so its tourism has to sell something else.
points: Ireland's cool, cloudy, wet and unreliable summer climate limits beach tourism and pushes Irish holidaymakers abroad.
Irish tourism instead markets scenery (the green landscape produced by the rain), culture, heritage, golf, walking, surfing and other outdoor activities.
The Wild Atlantic Way, a touring route of about 2,500 km along the west coast from Inishowen, Co. Donegal, to Kinsale, Co. Cork, was launched by Fáilte Ireland in 2014.
Domestic holidays rise in warm, sunny summers because fewer people go abroad for the sun.

notes.b: A warming climate changes where and when people take holidays, helping some places and hurting others.
points: Hotter Mediterranean summers bring heatwaves and wildfires that can deter or endanger tourists. In July 2023, wildfires on the Greek island of Rhodes forced thousands of tourists to be evacuated from resorts.
Visits may shift to spring and autumn, or to more northern destinations, possibly including Ireland.
Ski seasons shorten because there is less reliable snow.
Reefs bleach because seas warm, and islands face flooding because sea level rises.

notes.h: Other links between climate and development
notes.b: Climate also affects energy, health and productivity, and a final judgement on how far it controls development.
points: Energy: wind supplied about a third of Ireland's electricity in the early 2020s. Solar power is strong in sunny deserts, and hydroelectricity depends on high rainfall.
Climate also drives energy demand, for example heating in cold climates and air-conditioning in hot ones.
Health and productivity: tropical climates favour diseases such as malaria; extreme heat lowers the capacity for outdoor work; heatwaves kill.

Assessment: climate influences development but does not decide it alone. Rich countries with harsh climates, such as Israel, the Gulf states and Australia, overcome limits through capital and technology, while poor, rain-fed economies are the most vulnerable. Climate change widens this gap.
notes.tip: For an assess question, finish with a judgement: climate influences development, but technology and wealth modify it. Avoid saying climate determines development.

keyTerms.definition: Farming that depends on rainfall alone, without irrigation, and so is exposed to any shortfall in rain.
Farming based mainly on rearing livestock on grassland, such as dairy, beef and sheep.
A long period with much less precipitation than normal, so that water supply falls short of demand.
Land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas caused by climatic variations and human activities.
Turning sea water into fresh water for domestic use, used by rich dry countries where other supplies are short.
A shortage of water in rivers, reservoirs and groundwater.
Farmland left unplanted for a season so that it can recover or because water is short.
A line of trees planted to reduce wind erosion and protect crops and soil.

factCards.term: Irish agriculture: why grass is Ireland's most important crop
factCards.definition: Ireland's rain and mild temperatures give a long growing season: grass grows when soil temperature is above about 6 °C, which is most of the year, longest in the south and south-west. So most farmland is grassland for dairy, beef and sheep.

factCards.term: Irish farming: how rainfall shapes three farming regions
factCards.definition: Drier, sunnier south and east: tillage of barley, wheat, oats and potatoes (Co. Wexford, Carlow, Kildare). Golden Vale: moderate rain and brown earths suit intensive dairying. Very wet west and north-west: beef and sheep on rough grazing, small farms.

factCards.term: Irish farming: four problems caused by too much rain
factCards.definition: Cattle poach waterlogged soils, shortening the grazing season, so animals are housed and fed silage for longer, raising costs; silage, hay and cereal harvests are disrupted; nutrients leach and slurry runs off; damp favours potato blight and liver fluke.

factCards.term: Fodder crisis of spring 2013: causes and response
factCards.definition: The exceptionally wet summer of 2012 gave poor silage and hay harvests, and a cold, late spring in 2013 followed, so farmers ran out of feed. Fodder was imported, including from Britain and France, and the Government funded a fodder transport subsidy.

factCards.term: Summer 2018 drought: effects on Irish farming
factCards.definition: A long anticyclonic spell from late May to mid-July gave absolute drought at many stations. Grass almost stopped growing, so farmers fed winter fodder in summer and milk yields fell; Teagasc and the Government organised fodder imports for the following winter.

factCards.term: Egypt and the Nile: how the Aswan High Dam changed farming
factCards.definition: Egypt is almost rainless, so farming relies on Nile irrigation. The dam (1970) and Lake Nasser ended the flood's uncertainty, giving perennial irrigation, more than one crop a year and hydroelectricity; but silt is trapped, land salinised and the delta erodes.

factCards.term: California's Central Valley: irrigation and the 2012–2016 drought
factCards.definition: Dry summers mean fruit, nuts and vegetables need irrigation from state and federal water projects and groundwater. In the drought, land lay fallow and over-pumping caused land subsidence; Governor Jerry Brown ordered a 25% urban water cut in April 2015.

factCards.term: Ireland's water paradox: why Dublin is short of water
factCards.definition: Most rain falls in the west but most people live in the east, where rain is lowest (about 750 mm around Dublin); Dublin county had about 1.45 million of Ireland's 5.1 million people in 2022. Leaking pipes waste treated water; treatment capacity is tight.

factCards.term: Dublin's water supply: present sources and the planned project
factCards.definition: Mainly the River Liffey via the Poulaphouca reservoir (Blessington lakes) and the Vartry reservoir at Roundwood, Co. Wicklow. The planned, unbuilt Water Supply Project would pipe water about 170 km from the Shannon at Parteen Basin, south of Lough Derg.

factCards.term: Drought and household water in Ireland: the 2018 hosepipe ban and rural wells
factCards.definition: Irish Water imposed a hosepipe ban (Water Conservation Order) in the Greater Dublin Area in early July 2018, later extended nationwide. Rural homes on private wells and group schemes face wells running dry in drought and contamination after heavy rain.

factCards.term: Cape Town Day Zero: causes, measures and outcome
factCards.definition: Three dry winters (about 2015–2017) left reservoirs very low, and in early 2018 the city warned taps would be shut off. From 1 February 2018 use was capped at 50 litres per person per day; use roughly halved and Day Zero was avoided when the 2018 rains came.

factCards.term: Drought: economic effects to list
factCards.definition: Crop failure and livestock losses; higher food prices; lost farm income and rural jobs; famine and migration in poor countries; less hydroelectricity and cooling water for power stations; disrupted river transport; wildfires; government relief spending.

factCards.term: Millennium Drought, Australia: impacts and responses
factCards.definition: South-eastern Australia, roughly the late 1990s to 2009: farming in the Murray–Darling Basin was hit and towns faced water restrictions. Insurance, aid, water trading and technology absorbed losses; cities including Melbourne built desalination plants.

factCards.term: Horn of Africa drought, 2011: causes and first effects
factCards.definition: Two failed rainy seasons, linked to La Niña, brought drought across the Horn of Africa; crops failed, livestock died and food prices soared. The UN declared famine in parts of southern Somalia in July 2011.

factCards.term: Somalia famine, 2011: why it was so deadly and its toll
factCards.definition: Conflict (al-Shabaab) blocked food aid. A later UN-backed study estimated about 260,000 deaths in Somalia, about half of them children under five; large numbers fled to the Dadaab camps in Kenya and to camps in Ethiopia.

factCards.term: Ethiopian famine of 1983–85: causes and the world's response
factCards.definition: It followed drought and was worsened by civil war. It led to Band Aid (1984) and the Live Aid concerts (July 1985), organised by Bob Geldof.

factCards.term: Responses to drought: seven to name
factCards.definition: Early warning systems using rainfall, satellite and market data; water storage in dams, tanks and rainwater harvesting; drought-tolerant crop varieties; drip irrigation; food aid, cash transfers and insurance; restrictions such as hosepipe bans; desalination.

factCards.term: Sahel: economic effects of drought and desertification
factCards.definition: Droughts in the 1970s and 1980s brought failed harvests and livestock deaths; pastoralists lost livelihoods; food imports grew; people migrated to cities and abroad; herders and farmers clashed; Lake Chad has shrunk about 90% (widely quoted) since the 1960s.

factCards.term: Mediterranean sun tourism: why it grew and Spain's key figures
factCards.definition: Hot, dry, sunny summers; mass package tourism grew from the 1960s with cheap jet flights. Spain had about 85 million international tourists in 2023, a record, second only to France, and is the most popular foreign holiday destination for Irish people.

factCards.term: Sun tourism in Spain: problems linked to climate and overtourism
factCards.definition: Tourists come in the driest season, so water demand from hotels, pools and golf courses peaks when supply is lowest; jobs are seasonal; coasts are overdeveloped. In 2024 there were large protests against mass tourism in the Canary Islands and Barcelona.

factCards.term: Canary Islands: why they have a year-round tourist season
factCards.definition: They lie off north-west Africa at about 28° N; mild, dry winters and the cooling Canary Current attract northern Europeans in winter as well as summer.

factCards.term: Alpine ski tourism: how climate change threatens it and the responses
factCards.definition: It depends on reliable snow, but the snow line is rising and seasons are shortening, so lower resorts struggle or close. Resorts invest in snow-making, which needs water, energy and cold nights, and diversify into summer walking and cycling.

factCards.term: Hurricanes Irma and Maria (2017): the damage each caused
factCards.definition: Irma, a Category 5 hurricane in September 2017, damaged or destroyed almost every building on Barbuda, whose population was evacuated to Antigua. Maria, September 2017, devastated Puerto Rico, with about 3,000 deaths (official study).

factCards.term: Ireland's climate and tourism: limits and what Ireland markets instead
factCards.definition: Cool, cloudy, wet, unreliable summers limit beach tourism and send Irish people abroad. Ireland markets green scenery, culture, golf, walking and surfing, e.g. the Wild Atlantic Way, about 2,500 km from Inishowen to Kinsale, launched by Fáilte Ireland in 2014.

factCards.term: Climate change and Mediterranean tourism: heat and wildfire
factCards.definition: Hotter summers bring heatwaves and wildfires that deter or endanger tourists: in July 2023 wildfires on Rhodes forced thousands of tourists to be evacuated. Visits may shift to spring and autumn or to northern destinations, possibly including Ireland.

factCards.term: Climate and development: the judgement for an 'assess' question
factCards.definition: Climate influences development but does not decide it alone: rich countries with harsh climates, such as Israel, the Gulf states and Australia, overcome limits with capital and technology such as desalination, while poor rain-fed economies are most exposed.

questions.prompt: Climate characteristics have an influence on economic development. Discuss with reference to agriculture, drought and desertification, and tourism.
questions.model: Agriculture: in Ireland, grass is the main crop because of mild temperatures and rainfall of about 750 mm in the east to over 2,000 mm on western mountains. Too much rain waterlogs soils, shortens the grazing season and wrecks silage and hay, as in the wet summer of 2012, which caused the fodder crisis of spring 2013. Too little rain stops grass growing, as in the summer drought of 2018, when farmers fed winter fodder in summer. Globally, India's monsoon decides the farming year: rice is sown with the rains, a late or weak monsoon cuts harvests and incomes, and irrigation after the Green Revolution brought salinisation and waterlogging. Egypt depends on the Nile and the Aswan High Dam, completed in 1970, for irrigation. Drought and desertification: the Horn of Africa drought of 2011 followed two failed rainy seasons, crops failed, livestock died, food prices soared, the UN declared famine in parts of southern Somalia, and large numbers fled to camps in Kenya and Ethiopia. In the Sahel, a shortfall in the single wet season causes failed harvests, livestock deaths, loss of pastoralists' livelihoods, migration and conflict between herders and farmers over shrinking land and water. Tourism: hot, dry, sunny summers attract tourists to the Mediterranean, bringing jobs and foreign earnings, but tourists arrive in the driest season, so water demand peaks when supply is lowest. Spain is the most popular foreign holiday destination for Irish people. Climate also shapes Alpine skiing, where reliable snow supports resorts, but climate change shortens seasons and forces resorts to use artificial snow-making. Ireland's cool, wet summers limit beach tourism, so Irish tourism markets scenery and outdoor activities such as walking and surfing along the Wild Atlantic Way.

questions.prompt: Examine how climate characteristics influence economic development.
questions.model: Agriculture and water supply: in Ireland the east is driest but the population is concentrated there, so the water supply must be stored and piped; Dublin relies on the Wicklow reservoirs, and the planned Water Supply Project would pipe water from the Shannon. Leaking pipes and tight treatment capacity compound the problem. The 2018 drought led to a hosepipe ban. Globally, Cape Town's three dry winters left reservoirs very low and the city warned of Day Zero; limits of 50 litres per person per day, higher tariffs and campaigns cut use by about half, and the rains returned. Drought: California's Central Valley is productive because of irrigation, but its 2012–2016 drought led to groundwater over-pumping and land subsidence; a mandatory 25% cut in urban water use followed in 2015. In the developed economy, Australia responded with insurance, aid, water trading and desalination plants in Melbourne; in the Horn of Africa in 2011, two failed rainy seasons led to famine in parts of southern Somalia, where conflict blocked aid. Tourism: Spain, the most visited country after France, relies on climate-driven sun tourism; the Canary Islands have mild, dry winters for a year-round season; Ireland's Wild Atlantic Way markets the wet, green landscape. Assessment: climate influences economic development but does not decide it alone. Rich countries such as Israel, the Gulf states and Australia use desalination, technology and capital to overcome harsh climates, while poor, rain-fed economies such as those of the Sahel and the Horn of Africa are the most vulnerable, and climate change is widening this gap.

questions.prompt: Explain how rainfall levels influence agricultural activities in Ireland.
questions.model: Rainfall of about 750 mm in the driest east, about 1,000–1,250 mm across much of the west and over 2,000 mm on western mountains, and mild temperatures give Ireland a long grass-growing season, so most farmland is grassland used for dairy, beef and sheep. Grass grows when soil temperature is above about 6 °C. The drier, sunnier south and east suit tillage, such as barley, wheat, oats, potatoes and vegetables in Co. Wexford, Co. Carlow and Co. Kildare. The Golden Vale's moderate rainfall and good soils suit intensive dairying. The very wet west and north-west, with poorly drained soils, suit beef and sheep on rough grazing. Too much rain waterlogs soils, poaches grassland, shortens the grazing season and disrupts silage, hay and cereal harvests, as in the wet summer of 2012. Too little rain stops grass growing, as in the summer of 2018, when farmers fed winter fodder in summer.
